headings.title: Introduction and Hazards of Unsafe Injections
headings.content: Injection safety covers all activities involved in the administration of an injection, ensuring it causes no harm to the recipient, poses no risk to the provider, and results in safe waste disposal. Unsafe practices remain a major vector for bloodborne pathogen transmission in resource-limited settings. The primary hazards include accidental needle-stick injuries, reuse of disposable syringes, and incorrect medication preparation. When a contaminated needle pierces skin, pathogens such as Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and Human Immunodeficiency Virus pass directly into the bloodstream.

headings.title: Healthcare Workers as a Primary Risk Group
headings.content: Nurses, doctors, laboratory technicians, and midwives face daily occupational exposure to contaminated sharps. Needle-stick injuries occur most frequently during the recapping of needles, improper disposal of sharps containers, or during emergency procedures when urgency overrides caution. Junior nursing staff and students are statistically at higher risk due to a lack of clinical experience and manual dexterity under pressure.

headings.title: Patients and Care Recipients at Risk
headings.content: Patients receiving medical care expect healing, yet unsafe injections frequently introduce nosocomial infections. High-risk practices include reusing disposable equipment due to supply shortages, preparing medications in contaminated environments, and misusing multidose vials. Pediatric patients, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals suffer the most severe complications when exposed to contaminated injections.

headings.title: Waste Handlers and Community Risk Groups
headings.content:
- **Waste Collectors**: Sanitation workers who handle municipal trash containing improperly discarded medical sharps face high rates of accidental punctures.
- **Scavengers and Children**: Individuals foraging through open dumpsites or overflowing bins risk direct contact with protruding, uncapped needles.
- **Traditional Healers**: Informal practitioners operating outside formal regulatory oversight may reuse unsterilized injection equipment.

headings.title: Standard Precautions and Prevention Strategies
headings.content: Preventing injection-related transmission relies on consistent adherence to standard precautions. Every injection requires a sterile, single-use device and an aseptic technique. Healthcare workers must never recap needles using two hands. Safety-engineered devices, such as retractable needles or auto-disable syringes, physically prevent reuse and minimize accidental punctures. Used sharps must go immediately into puncture-resistant, leak-proof containers located close to the point of use.

headings.title: Post-Exposure Management Protocols
headings.content: When a needle-stick injury occurs, immediate action minimizes infection transmission. The injured staff member must wash the puncture site immediately with soap and clean water, avoiding scrubbing or bleeding expression. The incident requires prompt reporting to the infection control unit or occupational health officer. Assessment of the source patient's infection status dictates whether post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV or Hepatitis B immunoglobulin is necessary.
